title: Comments of Jacquelyn Omotalade re North American Electric Reliability Corporation's Petition for Approval of Revisions to its Rules of Procedure Regarding Computational Load under RR27-1.

documents.name: 1-RR27-1_Omotalade_Comment.pdf
documents.text:
Re: Docket No. RR27-1-000 - Comments on NERC's Petition for Approval of Revisions
to the NERC Rules of Procedure Regarding Computational Load

Dear Commissioners,

I write in my individual capacity as a Pennsylvania resident who works on sustainable
infrastructure and community development. My state is at the center of the data center build-out
this petition addresses: multiple gigawatt-scale campuses are now moving through Pennsylvania
permitting, and our Public Utility Commission is actively weighing how large-load costs and
reliability obligations should be allocated. I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed
Computational Load Owner and Computational Load Operator registry criteria.

I support the petition's core objective. Grid planners cannot manage what they cannot see, and the
rapid, software-driven load behavior NERC describes is a real planning problem. The proposed
thresholds - sites with total connected load of at least 50 MW supplied through equipment
connected to the Bulk Power System at 100 kV or above - reasonably target the facilities whose
behavior can affect bulk-system reliability, and NERC's decision to raise the threshold from 20
MW in response to stakeholder comment reflects a disciplined process. I offer three requests as the
Commission considers approval.

First, clarify treatment of behind-the-meter and grid-independent configurations. The proposed
criteria key registration to a site's electrical connection to the Bulk Power System, not to how much
power a site draws from it. A growing share of proposed campuses - including projects now
permitting in Pennsylvania - pair primary onsite generation with a grid interconnection used for
standby service, grid support, or export of excess power. The petition does not expressly address
these configurations. I ask the Commission to direct clarification that coverage turns on the
physical interconnection itself: a campus with onsite primary generation that nonetheless
interconnects at 100 kV or above should be registered, while a facility with no Bulk Power System
connection should not be swept in by ambiguity. Regulatory certainty on this point matters,
because developers are making design decisions now, and a registration regime that inadvertently
rewards disconnecting from the grid would undercut both reliability coordination and the grid
benefits these projects can provide.

Second, make registration data usable for state processes. State commissions are deciding siting,
cost-allocation, and tariff questions about these same facilities this year, not in the abstract. I ask
the Commission to consider how the registry can support - without duplicating or preempting -
state-level visibility into large computational loads, including appropriate public access to
non-sensitive registration information.

Third, sequence obligations sensibly. Registration should carry a reasonable compliance lead time,
should not apply retroactive burdens to operating facilities, and should stay coordinated with the
reliability standards under development in Docket No. RD26-7-000 so that registered entities face
a stable, coherent set of expectations.
 Thank you for the Commission's attention to the reliability dimensions of this load growth. Done
well, this registry can be the foundation for integrating large computational loads in a way that
protects both the grid and the communities hosting these facilities.

Respectfully submitted,

In community,
Jacquelyn Omosunbo Omotalade
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
